title: Modeling type 1 diabetes: the STZ model
objective: Explain how streptozotocin models type 1 diabetes and what controls an STZ experiment needs.

steps.title: Removing the β cells on purpose
steps.body: To study type 1 diabetes you need animals that have *lost* their **[[beta cell|β cells]]**. **[[streptozotocin|Streptozotocin]] (STZ)** does this chemically: it enters β cells and kills them, leaving the animal insulin-deficient and with high **[[blood glucose]]**. It's the standard way to model insulin-dependent diabetes in rodents.

visual.alt: Amber streptozotocin (STZ) molecules wait outside two neighbouring cells: a β cell whose membrane is studded with GLUT2 transporters, and a GLUT2-low neighbour with one. STZ is carried in through GLUT2, so the β cell takes up several molecules while the neighbour takes up only one, and the β cell's nuclear DNA breaks, marked with a coral cross and labelled 'DNA damage'. End state: the β cell is dead — greyed, dashed-outlined, blebbing and marked ✕ — and its insulin granules have stopped leaving for the capillary ('insulin ↓'), while the GLUT2-low neighbour survives (✓).
visual.caption: STZ rides in on GLUT2, so the cells carrying the most GLUT2 — β cells — take up the most and die.

steps.prompt: STZ kills β cells far more than most other cells. What makes it selective?
options: β cells take it up through their GLUT2 transporter, which they express heavily
β cells are simply far more fragile than any other cell type in the whole body
STZ is an antibody raised specifically against the β-cell surface proteins
It's injected straight into the pancreas, so only islet cells ever meet it
steps.explanation: STZ is a glucose analogue that enters mainly through GLUT2; β cells express a lot of GLUT2, so they take up a toxic dose and are killed (DNA alkylation), while GLUT2-low cells are relatively spared.

variants.setup: STZ enters cells through the GLUT2 glucose transporter.
variants.prompt: Which cells will it hit hardest?
options: Cells that express a lot of GLUT2
Cells with low GLUT2, which can't pump the STZ back out
Only cells that are actively dividing at the time
variants.reveal: GLUT2-high cells (β cells) take up the most STZ, which is the basis of its selectivity.

steps.prompt: Match each STZ dosing protocol to how it destroys β cells.
pairs: Direct chemical toxicity that kills β cells quickly
Immune-mediated insulitis that builds over days
steps.explanation: A single high dose kills β cells directly; repeated low doses (Like & Rossini) provoke [[insulitis]] — immune infiltration of the islet — which more closely resembles autoimmune type 1 diabetes.

steps.setup: You give one group of mice STZ and a control group the citrate buffer that STZ is dissolved in.
steps.prompt: What do you predict for the two groups?
options: STZ mice: high glucose and low insulin; buffer mice: roughly normal
Both groups end up about equally diabetic, just from the injection itself
The STZ mice stay normal while the buffer mice become the diabetic ones
STZ mice: high glucose and high insulin, since the pancreas compensates
steps.reveal: STZ destroys β cells → little insulin → glucose climbs. The vehicle (citrate buffer) controls for the injection itself, so those mice stay near normal — that contrast is how you know the phenotype is STZ, not handling.

variants.prompt: Why inject a control group with just the citrate buffer?
options: To control for the injection itself, isolating STZ's effect
To confirm the STZ dose was high enough to work
To give those control mice a milder form of diabetes
variants.explanation: The vehicle control shows the phenotype is due to STZ, not the handling or the solvent.

steps.prompt: Why be cautious using STZ when your study is about sensory neurons?
options: GLUT2 isn't limited to β cells, so STZ can act off-target, including on neurons
STZ is physically unable to enter any tissue other than the pancreas at all
Any neuron change must come from the high glucose, never from STZ itself
STZ has no effect on blood glucose, so the whole model is meaningless anyway
steps.explanation: GLUT2 is also in the kidney, liver and some glucose-sensing neurons in the brain, and direct STZ effects on neurons have been reported, so an STZ phenotype in a neuro study could partly reflect STZ's own off-target actions — not the diabetes alone.

flag.note: How much STZ's off-target (including neuronal) effects matter is debated; designs control for it differently.

variants.setup: Your mice are made diabetic with STZ, and you then study their sensory neurons.
variants.prompt: What's the main confound to rule out?
options: STZ's own direct effects on non-β-cell tissues, including neurons
That the mice were simply stressed by being handled during the injection
That high glucose itself, not the drug, changed the neurons
variants.reveal: STZ isn't perfectly β-cell-specific, so its direct effects are the confound to control for.

steps.title: Designing it well
steps.body: For a clean STZ study: always run the **vehicle control**, confirm diabetes by **[[blood glucose]]** (and ideally low insulin), and — because STZ isn't perfectly specific — consider a second, non-chemical way to make animals diabetic to cross-check. That rigor is exactly what makes an STZ result in a neuro-metabolic project convincing.
